title: Apollo Command Module (Block II)

sources.title: Apollo Experience Report: Spacecraft Hand Controller Development (NASA TN D-7884)
Translation Hand Controller (NASSP, Project Apollo for Orbiter)
Apollo 15 CSM Launch Checklist, index of panels (Apollo Flight Journal, NASA)
JoyPro cockpit catalog (panels, items and grip functions of the variant)

intro: The Apollo Command Module (1968-1975) carried three astronauts to the Moon and back. They sat on three couches side by side facing the big main display console; the commander on the left had the rotation hand controller at his right hand and the translation hand controller at his left. Below the couches was the navigation station with a sextant for star sightings. Panel numbers 2, 3, 5, 8, 122 and 225-229 are confirmed by a NASA checklist index; the other panel numbers and contents follow the operations handbook as known, not checked page by page.

areas.name: Main display console, panel 1
areas.text: Flight controls side in front of the commander.

panels.name: Main display console, panel 1 (commander)
panels.text: The flight control side of the main console in front of the commander in the left couch.
panels.context: The commander flies the spacecraft; the attitude ball and the abort lights are in front of him.

controls.name: FDAI 1
controls.text: The attitude ball (flight director attitude indicator): a ball with a horizon and markings that shows which way the spacecraft points, with needles for the turning rate and for the error to the wanted attitude.
controls.context: The crew pointed the spacecraft with it before every engine burn and for the return.

controls.name: Entry monitor system (EMS)
controls.text: A display with a speed-change counter for engine burns and a scrolling chart that shows the braking force and speed during the return through the atmosphere.
controls.context: It let the crew check the burns and the re-entry independently of the guidance computer.

controls.name: Launch vehicle and abort lights
controls.text: Lights for the engines of the Saturn rocket and the emergency detection system, which watched the rocket during launch.
controls.context: They helped the commander decide quickly whether to abort the launch.

controls.name: SCS attitude and control switches
controls.text: Switches for the backup attitude control (SCS, stabilization and control system): the attitude to hold, how fast the spacecraft may turn, and whether the SCS or the guidance computer (G&N) steers.
controls.context: The SCS took over when the guidance computer was not used. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Master alarm (CDR)
controls.text: A light that comes on with a tone when any system has a problem. Pressing it switches the alarm off.
controls.context: The caution and warning lights in the middle of the console then say which system it is.

controls.name: Event timer
controls.text: A timer that counts the time of engine burns and other events.
controls.context: The crew used it to time burns and the steps of the flight plan.

panels.name: Main display console, panel 2 (centre)
panels.text: The middle of the console: the caution lights, the propellant gauges, the keyboard of the guidance computer and the switches for separation and the parachutes.
panels.context: All three astronauts could see it; the guidance computer keyboard here was the busiest control of the flight.

controls.name: Caution and warning matrix
controls.text: A board of labelled lights, each saying which system has failed.
controls.context: When the master alarm sounds, the crew looks here to find the problem.

controls.name: SPS and RCS propellant indicators
controls.text: Gauges for how much fuel is left, and at what pressure, for the big main engine (SPS) and for the small steering jets (RCS).
controls.context: The SPS engine put the spacecraft into Moon orbit and brought it home, so its fuel was watched closely.

controls.name: DSKY
controls.text: The display and keyboard of the Apollo guidance computer. The astronaut types two-digit commands (VERB for an action, NOUN for the data) and reads the numbers it shows.
controls.context: The computer navigated and steered the spacecraft; the crew told it what to do through this keyboard.

controls.name: Mission timer
controls.text: A clock that shows the time since launch.
controls.context: The whole flight plan is written in time from launch.

controls.name: Sequential and earth landing system switches
controls.text: Switches for the big separation steps (from the rocket, from the service module), the docking equipment and the parachutes of the landing.
controls.context: They were used at fixed points of the flight plan. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

panels.name: Main display console, panel 3 (LM pilot)
panels.text: The systems side of the console: electricity, environment and radio.
panels.context: The astronaut in the right couch looked after these systems.

controls.name: Fuel cell controls and meters
controls.text: Switches and meters for the fuel cells, which make electricity and drinking water from hydrogen and oxygen. A purge cleans them.
controls.context: The fuel cells were the main source of electricity on the way to the Moon.

controls.name: DC and AC bus meters
controls.text: Meters that show the voltage of the electrical buses, the groups of electric lines that feed the equipment.
controls.context: A low reading warns that the power supply has a problem.

controls.name: Environmental control switches
controls.text: Switches for the cooling loops (a liquid that carries heat to radiators outside), the radiators and the cabin air.
controls.context: They kept the crew and the electronics at a safe temperature. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: S-band communications
controls.text: Switches for the S-band radio, which carried voice, data and television between the spacecraft and Earth.
controls.context: It worked all the way to the Moon through big antennas on the ground. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: SPS propellant pressure meters
controls.text: Meters for the pressure in the fuel and oxidizer tanks of the main engine (the oxidizer is what the fuel burns with).
controls.context: The engine only works when both tanks are pressurized correctly.

areas.name: Lower equipment bay
areas.text: The navigation station below the couches.

panels.name: Lower equipment bay (panel 122)
panels.text: The navigation station below the couches, where an astronaut could stand at the optics.
panels.context: Here the crew measured stars to correct the guidance platform, the device that keeps track of the spacecraft's attitude and speed.

controls.name: LEB DSKY
controls.text: A second keyboard and display of the guidance computer, next to the optics.
controls.context: The navigator used it while taking star sightings, without going back to the couch.

controls.name: Sextant and scanning telescope
controls.text: Optical instruments for measuring stars: a sextant for precise angles and a telescope with a wide view to find them.
controls.context: Star sightings let the computer correct its guidance platform and its position, as sailors once did with the stars.

controls.name: Optics controls
controls.text: Switches that choose how the optics are aimed (by hand or by the computer), set them to zero and drive them.
controls.context: They are used during the star sightings. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Minimum impulse controller
controls.text: An extra small rotation controller at the navigation station that fires the steering jets in tiny pulses.
controls.context: It turns the spacecraft very finely, for example to hold a star in the sextant.

areas.name: Side panels and circuit breakers
areas.text: Breakers and switches on the walls.

panels.name: Side panels and circuit breakers
panels.text: Circuit breakers and system switches on the side walls of the cabin.
panels.context: Most were set before launch; a tripped breaker is reset here.

controls.name: Panel 8 (left side)
controls.text: A panel on the left wall with circuit breakers (safety switches that cut power when something draws too much), the power of the backup attitude control and the floodlights.
controls.context: JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Panel 5 (right side)
controls.text: A panel on the right side with further system switches.
controls.context: JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Panels 225-229 (right equipment bay)
controls.text: Rows of circuit breakers in the right equipment bay.
controls.context: They protect the electrical lines of the systems; the crew checks them with the launch checklist.

controls.name: Audio control panels
controls.text: One audio panel for each astronaut (panels 9, 10 and 6) that sets which radios and the intercom he hears and talks on, and how loud.
controls.context: JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

areas.name: Hand controllers
areas.text: The rotation and translation hand controllers.

panels.name: Rotation hand controller
panels.text: The pistol grip on the right armrest of the commander's couch; the other couches have their own.
panels.context: It turns the spacecraft; the translation controller in the left hand moves it.

controls.name: Rotation hand controller (RHC)
controls.text: Moving the grip forward or back pitches the spacecraft, sideways rolls it, twisting yaws it. The turning speed follows how far the grip is moved (rate command).
controls.context: On a joystick it is the X, Y and twist axes; the crew used it for docking and for flying by hand.

controls.name: Push-to-talk switch
controls.text: While this switch on the grip is held, the astronaut's voice goes out on the intercom or the radio.
controls.context: It works like the button of a walkie-talkie; the grip is shaped for the left or the right hand.

panels.name: Translation hand controller
panels.text: The T-handle on the left armrest of the commander's couch.
panels.context: It moves the spacecraft without turning it; twisting it hands control to the backup system or aborts the launch.

controls.name: Translation hand controller (THC)
controls.text: This handle moves the whole spacecraft without turning it (translation): pushed in forward, pulled out back, and left, right, up and down, by firing the steering jets.
controls.context: It was used for docking with the Lunar Module; on a joystick it is a second three-axis controller.

controls.name: THC handle rotation
controls.text: Twisting the T-handle clockwise takes the guidance computer out of control and gives it to the backup system (SCS) and the manual engine steering; twisting it counter-clockwise starts a launch abort.
controls.context: These are emergency actions, which is why they sit on the handle the commander holds during launch.
